newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: War crimes prosecutor says cooperation improving.
newsitem.headline: War crimes prosecutor says cooperation improving.

text.p: The chief prosecutor for the international war crimes tribunal on former Yugoslavia said on Friday that she sensed an increased willingness by governments to cooperate and by victims to testify.

"I have, I think, a guarded optimism for the short term and an unguarded optimism for the long term" that those indicted will be brought to trial before the tribunal, Canadian judge Louise Arbour said after her first tour of the region.
She visited three of the republics that made up the former Yugoslav federation, which tore itself apart in the first half of this decade in the bloodiest conflict in Europe since World War Two.

So far, only seven out of more than 70 suspects indicted by the tribunal in The Hague are in custody. But Arbour told a news conference that progress was being made, giving the example of Serbia where three warrants were outstanding.
"There was no assertion by the government of any legal impediment to the government complying with its obligation to execute outstanding arrest warrants," she said after talks with Serbian ministers.
"We were advised on the other hand that domestic legislation had to be followed, which involved a court process.

"I have made it very clear that compliance is the primary objective and that we will be monitoring the speed and the efficiency with which the court process is assisting the execution of arrest warrants."

Arbour, appointed prosecutor in February 1996, said after visiting Bosnia, Croatia and Serbia that government officials had got the message that the West was serious about wanting suspected war criminals to face trial.

"I believe that the discussions I've had here reflect the understanding of the various government officials from all the jurisdictions I've visited -- a clear understanding...on that point," she said.
She also said that her meetings with aid organisations, diplomats and others indicated that victims of war crimes, which included massacres and the rape of civilians, were ready to testify.
"I am very happy to have found here an increased willingness on the part of victims of war crimes to turn to the tribunal to seek the kind of redress that they're entitled to," she said.
"I don't want to overstate that willingness, I believe that victims of the kind of trauma that the tribunal is investigating are entitled to have their plight treated with great sympathy.
"...But I sense a genuine willingness on the part of the victims to turn to the tribunal and cooperate with the tribunal in discharging its mission."

Arbour played down the significance of the fact that only a handful of those indicted so far were in custody while prominent indicted war figures, such as Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic, moved about publicly.
She said she had no contact with any "third party" or attorney representing Karadzic while she visited Pale, the Bosnian Serb base outside Sarajevo.
She refused to be drawn on other specific cases, saying she would not make "any public pronouncement (on) either the progress or existence of any ongoing investigations."
